name: Austro-Hungarian Empire

fields.foundation: The Austro-Hungarian Empire was founded not through conquest or dynastic expansion but by reorganising an existing state after military defeat. The Habsburg dynasty had governed Austria and its associated lands for centuries, but the defeats of the 1850s and 1860s forced a reconstruction of the imperial structure: the loss of Lombardy in the Second Italian War of Independence (1859), and the Austro-Prussian War of 1866, which excluded Austria from German affairs after the defeat at Königgrätz and cost it Venetia. The Ausgleich, or Compromise, of 1867 was negotiated between Emperor Franz Joseph I and Hungarian liberal leaders, above all Ferenc Deák and Count Gyula Andrássy, who recognised that a weakened Austrian Empire needed Hungarian cooperation and that Hungary could extract far-reaching autonomy from a dynasty in crisis. The result was the Dual Monarchy. It consisted of two distinct states, the Austrian half officially styled "the Kingdoms and Lands represented in the Imperial Council" (Cisleithania) and the Kingdom of Hungary (Transleithania). They shared a single monarch, crowned King of Hungary in Budapest in June 1867, a joint foreign ministry, a common army and common finances for these joint affairs, and a customs union renewed every ten years, while each maintained its own parliament, government, legal system and domestic policy. Franz Joseph had reigned since 1848 and would continue until his death in 1916. He was a man of deep personal conservatism and tenacity, and he held together a construction that tended to pull apart through longevity and bureaucratic discipline. The Compromise answered an acute problem, but it contained contradictions. It satisfied Hungarian aspirations while leaving the empire's other nationalities, Czechs, Slovaks, Poles, Ruthenians, Slovenes, Croats, Serbs, Romanians, Italians and others, without comparable autonomy, a permanent source of political tension.
fields.socioeconomy: Over the empire's fifty-one years the Austro-Hungarian economy moved from a predominantly agrarian base in 1867 towards one of the larger industrial economies of continental Europe by 1914. A single customs union held very different regions. In the industrialised provinces of Bohemia and Moravia, the Škoda works at Plzeň, textile mills, sugar refineries and glassworks made the region one of the most productive industrial zones in continental Europe. The Vienna basin was commercial, with banking, insurance and professional services. The plains of Hungary were among the great grain-producing regions of Europe, and Galicia, Bukovina, Dalmatia, Transylvania and, after 1878, Bosnia-Herzegovina had predominantly rural economies. The Bohemian lands supplied the greater part of the Austrian half's industrial output despite covering only a fraction of its territory, so that the developed north-west stood well ahead of the poorer east and south. Total output (GDP) roughly doubled between 1870 and 1913, with growth concentrated in Vienna, Budapest and Prague. Vienna's fin-de-siècle culture rested on this prosperity: the Ringstrasse, the Secession movement, coffee-house intellectual life and the professional class that produced Sigmund Freud, Gustav Mahler, Gustav Klimt and Theodor Herzl all belonged to a prosperous, cosmopolitan urban economy. Hungary's agricultural modernisation, meanwhile, made Budapest, formed in 1873 by the union of Buda, Óbuda and Pest, one of the world's great flour-milling centres, and the city grew to almost 900,000 inhabitants by 1910, one of the fastest-growing capitals in Europe.
fields.military: The Austro-Hungarian army was one of the most ethnically diverse in the world. It was commanded in German by an officer corps drawn from every nationality of the empire, and it was bound together by loyalty to the Habsburg dynasty rather than to any single nation. The common k.u.k. army (kaiserlich und königlich, Imperial and Royal), alongside the separate Austrian Landwehr and Hungarian Honvéd, drew conscripts from all the empire's peoples, and its regiments were so linguistically mixed that officers were expected to master the languages of their men. Regimental tradition and dynastic loyalty partly compensated for this fragmentation, and the army carried through the occupation and pacification of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1878, despite stiff local resistance, and the mobilisations of the Balkan crises before 1914. Its weaknesses became fully apparent only in industrial total war. Chief of Staff Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf's offensive planning was badly at odds with the army's real capabilities: in 1914 the invasions of Serbia were repulsed at Cer and the Kolubara, while in Galicia the army was routed around Lemberg (Lviv), losing much of its trained peacetime officer corps within months. The Brusilov Offensive of June to September 1916, launched by the Russian general Alexei Brusilov along a front of several hundred kilometres, inflicted well over half a million Austro-Hungarian casualties, including very large numbers of prisoners, a blow from which the army never fully recovered. Thereafter its operations depended heavily on German support, as at Caporetto in 1917, and the army's multinational character became a source of fragmentation as national loyalties increasingly superseded imperial ones.
fields.governance: The Austro-Hungarian system of government was among the most constitutionally complex in the world, because it had to accommodate great ethnic, linguistic and historical diversity within a single framework. The Dual Monarchy divided sovereignty between the emperor-king and two parliamentary systems, the Austrian Reichsrat in Vienna and the Hungarian Diet in Budapest, each sovereign within its own territory, while joint ministers for foreign affairs, war and the finances supporting them answered to Delegations drawn from both parliaments. Franz Joseph managed this system through personal authority, bureaucratic conservatism and, in Austria, the use of emergency decrees under Article 14 of the constitution when parliamentary deadlock made normal government impossible. He resorted to them more and more often in the fractious years before 1914. The empire's civil service was among Europe's most technically competent, administering taxation, public works, education and justice across some 676,000 square kilometres in a dozen official and recognised languages. Austria introduced universal male suffrage for the Reichsrat in 1907, while Hungary retained a narrow franchise that entrenched Magyar dominance. The central difficulty was the nationality question. The 1867 Compromise had satisfied the Hungarians but left Czechs, Slovaks, Croats, Romanians and other peoples in subordinate positions. This led to parliamentary obstruction, street protests and, especially in Bohemia, recurrent constitutional crises, most notoriously over the Badeni language ordinances of 1897. Attempts at federalisation or broader national rights were consistently blocked by German-speaking parties in Austria or by the Hungarian political elite, who feared any arrangement that might dilute their privileged position within the monarchy.
fields.impact: The Austro-Hungarian Empire's historical impact came largely through its dissolution, since the successor states and the settlements that followed its collapse governed Central European politics for the rest of the twentieth century. The empire's break-up in 1918 created or enlarged seven states, Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Poland, Romania and Italy, along lines that satisfied the principle of national self-determination only imperfectly. Large German-speaking minorities were left in Czechoslovakia and Hungarian minorities in Romania, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia. These and other grievances fuelled the irredentist politics of the interwar period and contributed to the conditions that produced the Second World War. The empire's most lasting contribution to European civilisation was cultural. Vienna at the turn of the twentieth century was one of the intellectual capitals of the Western world, producing the foundations of psychoanalysis (Freud), political Zionism (Herzl), the art of the Secession and Expressionism (Klimt, Schiele, Kokoschka), the Second Viennese School of music (Schoenberg, Berg, Webern), and the Austrian school of economics (Menger), while nurturing thinkers such as Ludwig Wittgenstein. Its legal and administrative infrastructure, including the Austrian civil code, the railway network and the postal system, persisted in modified form in the successor states and gave them institutional continuity through the political break. The customs union had for half a century bound together a market of more than fifty million people. Cutting its economic ties contributed to the prolonged economic disruption of the 1920s across Central Europe.
fields.decline: Fifty years of accumulated strain in the Austro-Hungarian Empire ended in four years of total war that it could not survive. The assassination of the heir to the throne, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 by the Bosnian Serb nationalist Gavrilo Princip triggered the July Crisis that produced the First World War. Austria-Hungary set this chain of events in motion with its deliberately unacceptable ultimatum to Serbia, calculating that German backing would allow a localised punitive war. The calculation proved catastrophic. The multinational army was unsuited to the demands of industrial total war: its logistics were overwhelmed, its reserves of trained officers were destroyed in the first campaigns, and its command struggled to maintain cohesion across many linguistic communities under sustained attrition. The Brusilov Offensive of 1916 broke the Habsburg army as an independent fighting force, and thereafter the empire was increasingly a junior partner to Germany. Franz Joseph's death in November 1916 removed the ruler whose personal authority had held the empire's contradictions in check. His young successor Karl I sought a negotiated peace through the secret Sixtus Affair of 1917 and in October 1918 offered to turn Austria into a federation of nationalities, but found neither Germany nor the Allies receptive. President Wilson's Fourteen Points of January 1918 called for the autonomous development of the peoples of Austria-Hungary, and the Allies' subsequent recognition of the Czechoslovak National Council encouraged the independence movements. In late October 1918 the empire dissolved from within: Czechoslovakia declared independence, the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs was proclaimed, and Hungary ended the union, while the Italian victory at Vittorio Veneto led to the armistice of Villa Giusti on 3 November. Karl I renounced participation in state affairs in November 1918 without formally abdicating, and the Habsburg dynasty's centuries of rule came to an end.
fields.summary: In its fifty-one years the Austro-Hungarian Empire was the home of some of the intellectual achievements that most changed the twentieth century, from Freud to Mahler and Klimt. It was also the state whose crisis over the assassination of its heir began the war that destroyed the old European order.
fields.teaser: The Dual Monarchy of 1867–1918 was one of Europe's most ethnically diverse states, home to a dozen or more nationalities. Its break-up after the First World War redrew Central Europe as a patchwork of new nation-states.
fields.t0: The 1867 Compromise turned the Habsburg lands into a Dual Monarchy: Austria and Hungary under one ruler, Franz Joseph.
fields.t1: Its Vienna produced Freud, Mahler, Klimt and Wittgenstein, while Bohemia became a major industrial region.
fields.t2: The war it began in 1914 broke its multinational army, and it dissolved into successor states in October 1918.
fields.dyk: Budapest was only created in 1873, by uniting Buda, Óbuda and Pest, and grew to almost 900,000 people by 1910.
